Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette:
Layla, a 38-year-old married housekeeper, presented for therapy reporting overwhelming anxiety and a sense of constant danger that had taken root six months prior. The precipitating event was an assault that occurred while she was walking home from a bus stop after a late shift. A man grabbed her from behind, dragged her into an alley, and pinned her against a brick wall. She remembers the terrifying feeling of powerlessness as he held her arms, his voice shouting threats close to her ear. The assault ended when a car’s headlights swept into the alley, startling the attacker, who then fled.

In the months that followed, Layla found that the memory of the event refused to settle. It existed not as a coherent story but as a collection of sensory fragments. Some moments were searingly clear: the rough texture of the brick against her cheek, the specific, profane words he shouted, and the sharp, radiating pain in her upper arms where his fingers had dug into her flesh. When these flashes returned, she reported that the ache in her arms would flare up with such intensity it felt as though she were being gripped all over again. Yet, great portions of the encounter were completely blank, leaving her with an unnerving sense that the worst parts were still hidden, waiting to emerge. This incomplete picture of the trauma reshaped her perception of the world. Because she could so vividly recall the pain of being held down, any situation where she felt forced to do something, no matter how benign, now felt like a terrifying violation. The memory of his shouting had tuned her ears to a specific frequency of danger, making any raised male voice feel like an immediate precursor to violence.

These sensitivities have made her daily life a minefield. A trigger, once encountered, launches her immediately into a state of acute threat. Last week, while she was cleaning a client’s home, the homeowner returned and yelled for his son from the entryway. For Layla, the sudden, booming sound transformed the quiet house into a space of imminent danger. Her heart began to race, and she reported backing into the corner of the bathroom she was cleaning, her eyes darting towards the small window, her mind consumed with scanning for an escape route. Her concentration shattered, and she spent the next hour unable to focus, simply wiping the same countertop repeatedly, listening for footsteps on the stairs. She has come to believe that safety is an illusion and that threat is everywhere, just waiting for a moment of inattention.

This pervasive sense of threat now dominates her existence, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of hypervigilance. At home, she spends her evenings listening intently for any sound that might signal an intruder, unable to relax until her husband has double-checked every lock. This constant state of alert, this perpetual scanning for danger, has made her more likely to find it. While trying to watch television, her heightened threat-monitoring causes her to fixate on news reports of other assaults, which serve as reminders of her own status as a victim and send her spiraling. Her intense focus, meant to protect her, has instead made her world smaller and more frightening, ensuring that a trigger is never far away. The strain has become palpable in her marriage; her husband feels he is walking on eggshells, afraid that a simple request or a moment of frustration will send his wife into a panic. It was after he found her frozen in place, staring at the front door for nearly an hour after a car backfired on their street, that they agreed she needed to seek help. She came to therapy stating, through tears, that she feels she is losing her mind and is desperate to feel safe in her own home again.
